opus-5.5.text:
I actually think it makes ML systems research more important, not less, though the nature of the work shifts.

When people see the field converging on transformer-style architectures and a handful of frontier models, the natural reaction is, "Great, the problem is solved. Just optimize that one thing really well and you're done." There's some truth to that. Having a stable target lets you go much deeper. You can hand-tune kernels, co-design hardware, and squeeze out every bit of efficiency because you know the workload won't change completely next month.

But I see a few reasons why systems become even more central.

First, when the model architecture stabilizes, the differentiation moves into the system. If everyone runs roughly the same kind of model, then the question becomes who can serve it cheaper, faster, with lower latency, on more kinds of devices. That is purely a systems question. The cost of inference at scale is huge, so a 2x efficiency gain is worth an enormous amount of money and energy.

Second, convergence at the top doesn't mean uniformity at deployment. You have the same model family running on data center GPUs, on different accelerators, on laptops, on phones, in the browser. Each environment has different memory constraints, compute characteristics, and programming models. Bridging one model to all that hardware diversity is exactly the problem machine learning compilers and runtimes are meant to solve. That's a lot of what motivated our work on things like TVM and later MLC-LLM: write it once and get it running well everywhere.

Third, "converged" is always temporary. Even within transformers there's constant change: attention variants, mixture of experts, long context, quantization schemes, speculative decoding, and now agentic workloads that look very different from a single forward pass. If your whole stack is hand-written for one snapshot, you get stuck. So there's a real need for systems that are productive and flexible, not just fast for one fixed case. Balancing that, being as good as hand-tuned code while staying adaptable, is the interesting research problem.

And finally, I think the scope of ML systems is expanding. It used to mean "make training or inference fast." Now it includes how you structure generation, how you do constrained decoding and structured output, how models interact with tools and with each other, how you manage KV caches across many requests. The model becomes one component in a bigger system, and designing that bigger system well is a systems problem.

So my view is that convergence changes the questions, but it raises the stakes. When a few models are used by everyone, every improvement in the underlying system gets multiplied across the whole world.

r001.rationale: It discusses supporting models across diverse hardware and co-designing hardware, but does not say software must adapt across successive generations from the same vendor.

r002.rationale: It describes the same model family running on different hardware, without stating that different hardware generations favor different models.

r003.rationale: It argues that systems research is becoming more important and mentions hardware co-design, but does not connect that importance to increasing interdependence between hardware and models.

fable-5.1.text:
I actually think it makes systems research more important, not less, and maybe that sounds counterintuitive so let me explain.

When you have a lot of model diversity, people kind of tolerate inefficiency, because everything is changing anyway. You write a kernel for one architecture and next month there's a new architecture. But when the field converges, say around transformer-style models with a handful of common operators, suddenly the cost of running those models at scale becomes the whole game. Everyone is running basically the same computation, so every percent of efficiency you get in the system is multiplied across the entire industry. That's actually what happened with convolutions, right? Once ResNet-style models became dominant, there was this enormous investment in making those specific patterns run fast, and that investment paid off because it was shared.

The other thing is that convergence on the model side doesn't mean convergence on the hardware side. If anything we're seeing more hardware diversity: different GPUs, TPUs, Apple silicon, phones, browsers through WebGPU. So you have this interesting situation where the model is relatively fixed but the deployment targets are exploding. That's really a systems problem. How do you take one model and make it run well everywhere without hand-tuning for each backend? That's the kind of question we try to tackle with things like TVM and MLC, and I think it gets more pressing, not less.

And then there's the question of who gets to run these models. If only a few big labs can serve a dominant model, that's a very centralized world. Systems research is one of the main levers for changing that, because if you can get a strong model running on a laptop or a phone, you've changed the economics and the access story. So I'd say the model side consolidating actually sharpens what systems people should be working on. The targets are clearer, and the stakes are higher.

r001.rationale: It discusses growing hardware diversity and adapting deployment across targets, but does not say successive generations from the same vendor require software adaptation.

r002.rationale: It describes model convergence and deployment across different hardware, but does not state that the best model changes between hardware generations.

r003.rationale: It argues that systems research becomes more important as deployment targets diversify, but does not connect increasing hardware–model interdependence to the need for a systematic view of ML systems.

astra-6.text:
I think even if we converge toward a few dominant models, that doesn’t mean we converge toward a single way of running them. The same model might be deployed in a data center or on a phone, with very different requirements for latency, memory, cost, and privacy. Those differences create a lot of interesting systems problems.

In fact, having a few widely used models can make systems research more impactful, because an improvement in efficiency can benefit many applications. It also creates an opportunity for specialization: once you understand the workload, you can optimize across the model, compiler, runtime, and hardware.

But I would be careful about assuming that today’s architectures will stay fixed. The challenge is to take advantage of what is stable while building systems that can adapt as models evolve. So I see convergence as shifting the focus of ML systems research, rather than making it less important.

sol-6.1.text:
I think ML systems research becomes even more important. If many applications converge on a few model architectures, then improving the systems that run those models has a very large impact. A reduction in inference cost or latency can benefit a lot of people.

But convergence at the model level does not mean convergence at the systems level. You still have different hardware, different latency requirements, and different deployment environments. Serving a model in a data center is a different problem from running it on a phone. And even with the same model, the workload can vary quite a bit.

So I think the research questions shift. We can specialize more around common workloads, but we also need good abstractions that let us adapt when models and hardware change. That balance between specialization and flexibility remains a very interesting systems problem.

r001.rationale: The response mentions different hardware and adapting as hardware changes, but does not say successive generations from the same vendor require software adaptation.

r002.rationale: The response does not compare which models suit different hardware generations.

r003.rationale: It says ML systems research and adaptable abstractions remain important, but does not connect increasing hardware–model interdependence to the need for a systematic view of ML systems.
